section.title: Do Not Neglect Such a Salvation
section.sectionRationale: The first of the letter's five warning passages. Having proved the Son's supremacy, the writer draws the urgent 'therefore': if a word given through angels was binding, how much more the salvation announced by the Lord Himself. The danger is not violent rebellion but quiet drifting.
section.thesis: Because the Son is so superior to the angels, the salvation He announced carries far greater weight than the law given through angels; to neglect it is to drift toward inescapable judgment, so we must pay all the closer attention.
section.frameNote: A single argument from lesser to greater: the reliability of the message spoken by angels, then the far greater accountability for the salvation announced by the Lord, confirmed by eyewitnesses and attested by God with signs.

verses.text: We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not {{pararreo|drift away}}.
For if the message spoken by angels was {{bebaios|binding}}, and every transgression and disobedience received its just punishment,

units.label: So great a salvation, so confirmed

verses.text: how shall we escape if we neglect such a great {{soteria|salvation}}? This salvation was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him,
and was affirmed by God through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His will.

pararreo.gloss: To drift, slip, or flow past, like a boat carried off course or a ring slipping from a finger. The danger the writer names is not a deliberate leap into apostasy but a slow, unnoticed drifting away from what has been heard.

bebaios.gloss: Firm, reliable, legally binding and valid. The law given through angels was binding, and its violations were justly punished; the argument runs from the lesser binding word to the greater and weightier salvation in the Son.

soteria.gloss: Salvation, rescue, deliverance. Here it is 'so great a salvation', announced by the Lord Himself, confirmed by eyewitnesses, and attested by God with signs and gifts of the Spirit. Its greatness makes neglecting it all the more perilous.

basic.context: This is the letter's first warning. The writer has shown that the Son is greater than the angels who mediated the law at Sinai. Now he presses the point home: if breaking the law given through angels brought just punishment, how much more serious to ignore the salvation the Lord Himself announced. The peril is drifting, slowly slipping away, rather than openly rejecting.
basic.hermeneutics: Read this as pastoral warning, not cold threat. The 'we' includes the writer; it is a family being urged to hold on. The argument moves from lesser to greater: greater messenger, greater message, greater accountability.
basic.originalLanguages: The key verb is pararreō, to drift away like a ship off course. The law was bebaios, binding and valid. The gospel is so great a sōtēria, salvation, that to neglect it is to court a judgment none can escape.
basic.typology: The word at Sinai, mediated through angels, was a shadow of the greater word now spoken by the Lord. The eyewitnesses and confirming signs echo how God authenticated His word in earlier ages, now surpassed in the confirmation of the gospel.
basic.christ: Christ is the Lord who first announced this salvation. What the prophets and angels foreshadowed, He proclaimed in person, and His message is confirmed by those who heard Him and by God's own attesting power.
basic.god: God is just: transgression rightly receives its penalty. God is also generous, confirming the gospel with signs, wonders, miracles, and gifts of the Spirit, so that we have every reason to hold fast rather than drift.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 12 warns against refusing Him who speaks. Deuteronomy honours the binding law given at Sinai. Acts records the signs and wonders that confirmed the apostles' witness.
basic.oneStory: God's saving word runs through the whole Bible, growing in clarity until the Lord Himself announces salvation. This warning calls each generation not to let that word slip past unheeded.

context.literary:
Hebrews 2:1-4 is the first of the five warning passages in the letter, and it shows the pattern the writer will follow throughout. He lays down a stretch of exposition, here the seven quotations of chapter 1, and then turns to exhort. The turn is marked by 'therefore,' and by a shift from 'He says' to 'we.' The whole thing is one argument, and the exhortation is not an interruption of the doctrine but its purpose. The writer believes in the Son's superiority because he wants his readers to stay.

The unit is a compact argument from lesser to greater, the pattern the rabbis later called light and heavy. It has three steps. First comes the premise: the word spoken through angels was binding, and every breach of it met its just penalty, verse 2. Then the inference: if that is so, how shall we escape if we neglect a salvation that is greater, verse 3? Then the grounds that make the salvation greater: it was first spoken by the Lord Himself, confirmed to us by those who heard, and witnessed to by God with signs and gifts, verses 3 and 4. The writer is careful to put the strongest term last, 'neglect,' and to give it an object that cannot be matched: 'such a great salvation.'

Notice that the unit is built as a chain of three links: the Lord, those who heard, and God confirming. Each link is mentioned in order, so that the readers are placed at the end of the chain, on the receiving side of a word that began with Jesus Himself.

Notice, too, the movement of the opening line. The writer says 'we must,' joining himself to his readers, and uses a comparative, 'closer attention,' as if their attention had already begun to slacken. The danger he names is slow. The verb he picks, drift, belongs to the sea. No one in the passage rebels. They slip.

Finally, the unit marks a transition. Chapter 1 argued from the Son's glory, and the second chapter will argue from His humiliation: 'made lower than the angels' for a time, 2:9. The warning sits between them like a pause between two movements.
context.historical:
The readers belonged to a second generation. The writer says the message was 'confirmed to us by those who heard Him,' which places both himself and his hearers at one remove from the apostles' eyewitness. That fits what we know of the churches a generation after Pentecost. The first heralds had spoken in person, Luke 1:1-2 speaks of the 'initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word,' and by now the faith was handed down. Paul's own situation was different: he insisted that he had received his gospel directly from Christ, Galatians 1:12, while the author of Hebrews places himself in the line of those who heard it from others.

The signs and wonders he mentions fit the pattern in Acts. Paul and Barnabas at Iconium were 'speaking boldly for the Lord, who affirmed the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders,' Acts 14:3. Mark's Gospel ends with the same idea, that the Lord worked with the apostles 'confirming His word by the signs that accompanied it,' Mark 16:20. The confirmation of the gospel by miracles was not meant to dazzle but to authenticate the message, in the way that signs had authenticated Moses before Pharaoh, Exodus 4:1-9.

The 'word spoken by angels' sends us back to the way Jewish tradition and the New Testament understood Sinai. Stephen charges his hearers with receiving the law 'ordained by angels' and not keeping it, Acts 7:53, and Paul says it was 'administered through angels by a mediator,' Galatians 3:19. The earlier law was strict. Hebrews 10:28 says that anyone who rejected the law of Moses died without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses. The writer's readers knew exactly what the old penalties were, which gives his 'how shall we escape' its weight.

The danger of drifting reflects a real pressure. The letter later mentions public insult and confiscated property, Hebrews 10:32-34, and a habit among some of staying away from the gathering, Hebrews 10:25. For Jewish believers the old rituals offered a recognised and protected place within the empire, while the new faith did not. Slipping back was understandable, and that is why the writer treats it as the real risk.
context.canonical:
The warning in 2:1-4 is the first of a series. Hebrews 3:7 to 4:13 warns from the failure of the wilderness generation, Hebrews 5:11 to 6:12 from slow growth and falling away, Hebrews 10:26-31 from deliberate sin against the Son, and Hebrews 12:25-29 from refusing the one who speaks from heaven. Reading them together shows that 2:1-4 is the mildest and the shortest. It speaks of drift and neglect, and the later ones sharpen that into hardening, falling away and trampling the Son of God. The progression suggests that the writer is describing a road with steps down.

The Old Testament itself supplies a model. After Sinai Moses warned Israel that the one who sinned defiantly 'has despised the word of the LORD,' Numbers 15:30-31, and Deuteronomy rests its warnings on the conviction that God's word spoken at Horeb is life or death. The prophets repeatedly charged the people with not listening, Jeremiah 7:13 and Zechariah 7:11-12. In that line, Hebrews 2:1-4 asks whether those who have the Son will repeat the old pattern.

The theme of hearing and doing runs through the New Testament. Jesus said that anyone who hears His words and does them is like a wise man who built on rock, Matthew 7:24-27, and James warns against hearing the word without doing it, James 1:22-25. The parable of the sower speaks of seed that is choked or snatched away, Mark 4:14-19. In the same family belong Paul's call to 'continue in your faith, established and firm,' Colossians 1:23.

Hebrews 12:25 closes the circle. 'See to it that you do not refuse Him who speaks. For if the people did not escape when they refused Him who warned them on earth, how much less will we escape if we reject Him who warns us from heaven?' The same form of argument appears there as here, which suggests that the whole letter is built around these two warnings, the first near the beginning and the last at the end.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer wants his readers to feel the weight of what they have been given, and to be awake to the slow loss of it. He does not accuse them of apostasy. He says 'we,' and the verb he uses is gentle: drift. The warning is therefore not a threat but a shepherd's call to hold fast to what is most precious.

He also intends to turn the greatness of the Son, argued in chapter 1, into a reason for attention. A reader who has just been told that the Son made the universe and sits at God's right hand cannot treat His message as one more religious option. The reasoning is simple and strong: the more glorious the speaker, the more serious the hearing. This is the opposite of a casual faith that assumes the gospel can be put aside and retrieved at will.

Behind these lines is a pastoral concern for what happens to people whose faith is under pressure. The writer knows that Christians seldom leave in one dramatic act. They stop reading, stop meeting, stop praying, and then one day find they are far from shore. His purpose is to catch them while it is still a matter of drifting, and to restore their attention to the Lord who spoke.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage is prescriptive: it gives a command and a warning. The command, to pay closer attention, is addressed to every generation of believers. But how it applies is easy to misread in either direction.

Some read the warning as a reason to doubt whether they are saved at all, and lose their peace over every dry season. The writer does not mean that. His 'we' includes himself, and the tone is of a friend shouting a warning, not a judge pronouncing a sentence. Others read the warning as irrelevant to anyone who is truly saved, and so ignore it. The writer does not mean that either, since the letter treats the warnings as real. What the text prescribes is attention: to hear the gospel again, to remain among God's people, to take the word seriously.

It should also be noted that the reference to signs, wonders and miracles describes how the gospel was confirmed in the first generation and is not a command to seek or reproduce them. Christians differ on whether such signs continue, and the passage does not settle it. What it does say is that God Himself gave the confirmation, and that believers rest on His testimony, not their own.

debates.question: Can a true believer 'drift away' and be lost?

views.label: God keeps His people, and uses warnings as one means
views.case: Passages such as John 10:28-29 and Philippians 1:6 teach that those the Father gives to the Son are not lost. The warnings are real and work as the very means by which God preserves. The elect take heed and persevere. Hebrews itself speaks of Christ's offering perfecting forever 'those who are being sanctified,' Hebrews 10:14, and says He is able to save completely those who draw near, Hebrews 7:25.

views.label: Those who fall away show they never truly belonged
views.case: First John 2:19 says of those who left that 'they did not belong to us.' On this reading, drifting is the evidence of an empty profession, and the warning exposes it. The letter also says we share in Christ 'if we hold firmly to the end,' Hebrews 3:14, a way of saying that endurance proves reality.

views.label: A true believer can fall away and be lost
views.case: Some read Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26-29 as describing people who really were enlightened, shared in the Holy Spirit and tasted the heavenly gift, and then fell. They argue that the warnings would be empty if the danger were not real for believers, and that the language of the passages describes genuine participation.

debates.bearing: Christians have differed over this for centuries, and Hebrews gives all sides something to work with. On every reading the command is the same: do not drift, hold fast, listen. The text does not invite anyone to presume on grace while their attention fades, and it does not invite the sincere believer to despair.

debates.question: What does it mean that the law was 'spoken by angels'?

views.label: A tradition rooted in the Greek and Hebrew text of Moses
views.case: Deuteronomy 33:2 mentions holy ones with the Lord at Sinai, and the Greek version speaks of angels. Exodus 19 describes thunder and the trumpet but not angels by name. The New Testament writers, Acts 7:53 and Galatians 3:19, accept the tradition as true.

views.label: A Jewish tradition used by the writers as a shared assumption
views.case: Some argue that the idea of angels mediating the law is a Second Temple development which the New Testament authors took over without endorsing every detail, since their point lies elsewhere: the Son is greater than any mediator.

debates.bearing: The argument does not depend on settling this. Whatever role angels had, the writer's readers accepted it, and the contrast stands: a message through servants was binding, so a message through the Son is more so.

study.originalLanguages:
Several words in these four verses repay close attention, and some of their links are easy to miss in English.

The verb that opens the unit, prosechein, 'to pay attention,' is literally to hold the mind toward something, to turn it in a direction and keep it there. The comparative perissoteros, 'more earnestly' or 'closer,' suggests an abundance of attention, more than before. The writer is not asking for a new activity but for more of what they were doing.

The verb pararreo, 'to drift away,' is where the image becomes vivid. It is found only here in the New Testament. It means to flow past or slip by, as a ring slips off a finger, or a boat past its landing. The Greek translation of Proverbs 3:21 uses it for a son who must not let wisdom slip from his sight, which the BSB renders 'do not lose sight of this.' The danger is not that the readers hurl the gospel away but that it flows past them while they look elsewhere.

Next, the pair of words for the law's breach. 'Transgression,' parabasis, is stepping across a line. 'Disobedience,' parakoe, is a compound of the word for hearing, akouo, and means something like 'hearing amiss' or refusing to listen. The pairing mirrors the passage's concern with hearing, for the readers are told to attend to what they have 'heard,' and the sin of the old generation was a failure to hear. The reward language is also deliberate. The 'just punishment' is misthapodosia, a word for recompense that the letter uses elsewhere for reward, Hebrews 10:35 and Hebrews 11:26. The same word covers what the faithful receive and what the disobedient meet. God's dealings are exactly proportionate either way.

The adjective bebaios, 'binding,' means firm and valid, as of a guarantee. In verse 2 the word spoken by angels was bebaios. In verse 3 the gospel was ebebaiothe, 'confirmed,' from the same root. The writer is deliberately setting the two side by side: the old word was made firm by penalties, and the new word is made firm by witnesses. The grammar invites a reader to see that the new is no less firm.

The word amelesantes, 'if we neglect,' is a participle of a verb that means to take no care. It is the word of the person who does not trouble to turn up. Notice that the writer does not say 'if we reject' or 'if we deny.' He chooses the quietest possible sin, and says it is enough. The same verb appears in Paul's charge to Timothy, 'Do not neglect your gift,' 1 Timothy 4:14.

Verse 3 calls the salvation telikaute, 'so great,' a word of size and importance. 'Salvation,' soteria, becomes the keyword of the whole letter, and its last use in this section comes at 1:14 'those who will inherit salvation.' The relative clause says the salvation 'began to be spoken through the Lord,' with the verb arche, 'beginning,' pointing to the origin. Salvation is not a human invention; it started in the mouth of Jesus.

Finally, verse 4 uses the double-compound verb synepimartyreo, 'bearing witness together with.' God joins His own testimony to that of the apostles. He adds 'signs, wonders and various miracles,' three words used together in Acts 2:22, with poikilai, 'various,' stressing their variety, and 'distributions of the Holy Spirit,' merismoi. The same noun, merismos, appears at Hebrews 4:12 of the word that divides soul and spirit. And the gifts are given 'according to His will,' thelesin, His own willing, so the Spirit's gifts are no human achievement.

typology.type: The law given at Sinai through angels
typology.fulfillment: At Sinai God spoke from the mountain with fire, thunder and a trumpet, Exodus 19:16-19, and the people begged that the word not be spoken to them directly, Exodus 20:19. The law was the covenant's foundation and came with severe penalties, as Hebrews 10:28 recalls. In Christ the correspondence escalates: the one who speaks now is not an angel or Moses but the Lord Himself, and He speaks from heaven, Hebrews 12:25. The type falls short because the old covenant could not make anyone perfect, Hebrews 7:19, and it was administered by servants. The new word is more serious and also more gracious.

Israel was brought out of Egypt by signs and wonders yet drifted into unbelief in the wilderness, and the writer will make this explicit in Hebrews 3:7 to 4:13. They are a pattern of what happens when a people who have seen great works fail to hold on to the word. Paul reads the same history as an example for us in 1 Corinthians 10:1-11. The type falls short in that the generation fell short of the land, whereas the readers are in danger of falling short of the true rest, Hebrews 4:1, and of a salvation that the earlier rescue only symbolised.

typology.type: Moses and the signs that authenticated his word
typology.fulfillment: God gave Moses signs to show Pharaoh and Israel that He had really sent him, Exodus 4:1-9 and Exodus 4:30-31. The confirmation of the gospel by signs, wonders and gifts follows that pattern. In Christ the escalation is from servant to Son, a point that Hebrews 3:1-6 will develop. The type falls short because Moses' signs confirmed a messenger who would die, while the signs of the gospel confirm a word whose speaker lives and reigns.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ in a quiet and revealing way, for it names Him as the first herald of the salvation. 'This salvation was first announced by the Lord.' The Greek says that it 'received its beginning of being spoken through the Lord,' and the writer does not say that Jesus merely taught about salvation as other teachers might. The gospel began in His mouth. Mark's Gospel records Him beginning His ministry by proclaiming the good news of God, Mark 1:14-15, and Luke records Him reading Isaiah in the synagogue and saying, 'Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing,' Luke 4:21. The one who announces the salvation is also the one who accomplishes it.

That points to a feature of Christ's person. Prophets spoke of salvation in the future tense. Jesus spoke of it as present. When Zacchaeus received Him, He said, 'Today salvation has come to this house,' Luke 19:9. The word that the angels delivered at Sinai was a word of law; the word that the Lord delivered is a word of rescue. That is why the writer can call it 'so great a salvation.' It is great in the greatness of its speaker, and great in what it gives: deliverance from sin and from the fear of death, which chapter 2 will name, Hebrews 2:14-15.

The passage also shows Christ as the one who is heard through others. The eyewitnesses who passed on His word are not a substitute for Him, and their testimony does not replace His. They transmit His voice. This is the logic of the apostolic witness: Jesus said, 'Whoever listens to you listens to Me,' Luke 10:16. The believer who reads the New Testament is hearing, through the apostles, the Lord who first spoke, and that is why drifting from the word is drifting from Him.

God's own confirmation of the message is also about Christ. The signs, wonders and gifts of the Holy Spirit do not draw attention to themselves. They are the Father's testimony to the Son, as in the Gospel of John, where Jesus says the works He does bear witness to Him, John 5:36. And the gifts of the Spirit come because the Son has been exalted and has sent the Spirit, Acts 2:33.

The warning is in the end a call to a person. 'Neglect' is not a failure to follow a system, but a failure to respond to the Lord. The writer will go on to show that this Lord is merciful and faithful, who 'is able to help those who are being tempted,' Hebrews 2:18, so the one whom the readers are tempted to ignore is the one who most understands them. The sternness of the warning is sustained by the tenderness of the Saviour.
study.god:
The passage shows God as just. The writer takes it for granted that the law was binding and that every breach 'received its just punishment.' The God of Hebrews is not indifferent to disobedience. The word 'just' here is a legal one and speaks of a verdict that fits the offence. Divine justice is not arbitrary, and it is not abolished by grace. This holds the gospel's seriousness: the same God who gave the law is the one who gives the greater word, and He will not be mocked, Galatians 6:7.

The passage shows God as the author of salvation. The unit is full of verbs of divine action even when God is not the grammatical subject: the salvation was announced by the Lord, confirmed by witnesses, and 'affirmed by God' with signs and gifts. Salvation is not something people reach by effort, but something that comes down in speech and is attested by deed. The initiative is God's from beginning to end.

God also appears as the one who gives testimony. The compound verb of verse 4 says that God bears witness alongside the apostles. This is a remarkable idea: the Lord of heaven does not leave His message to stand on its own, but vouches for it with His own deeds. The pattern matches the book of Acts, where the apostles preach and God confirms. It also shows God's patience with the weakness of human faith, for He gives evidence to those who need it, as He did for Moses.

God is generous in the distribution of His gifts. The Spirit's gifts are given 'according to His will,' and Paul says the same: the Spirit 'apportions them to each one as He determines,' 1 Corinthians 12:11. This guards believers from pride and envy. No one earns a gift, and no one lacks the Spirit's presence.

The unit also holds justice and generosity together without letting either go. If the God who is just was the one who gave Sinai's penalties, the God who is generous is the one who gives signs and the Spirit. The heaviness of the warning comes from the size of the gift. A wise reader will not take the generosity as a reason to presume, nor the justice as a reason to fear.

For worship, the passage asks for attentive listening. It makes the hearing of the word, in preaching, in Scripture reading, in the gathered church, a serious act before God, to be done with the care of those who know who is speaking. The God who speaks in the Son expects to be heard, and He is worth hearing.

crossReferences.note: The mirror of this warning, near the letter's end. The people who refused the one who warned on earth did not escape, so how much less will we if we refuse the one who warns from heaven. The same lesser-to-greater reasoning links the beginning and the end.

Whoever rejected the law of Moses died without mercy, so how much more severely will one be punished who has trampled the Son of God. It shows the specific penalties the writer has in mind in 2:2 and how the argument sharpens from neglect to contempt.

Stephen accuses his hearers of having received the law ordained by angels and not keeping it. It confirms that angelic mediation at Sinai was an accepted tradition in the early church and shows that having a great law is no guarantee of keeping it.

Paul says the law was administered through angels by a mediator, added because of transgressions. It supports the claim of verse 2 that the law came by angelic agency and adds that it was meant to point to the coming seed, who is Christ.

Luke speaks of the things handed down by the initial eyewitnesses and servants of the word. This is the same chain of testimony as 'confirmed to us by those who heard Him,' a second generation receiving the gospel from those who were there.

The Lord worked with the apostles and confirmed the word by the signs that accompanied it. It is the closest Gospel parallel to verse 4 and shows the pattern of preaching followed by divine confirmation.

Paul and Barnabas spoke boldly, and the Lord affirmed the message of His grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders. It gives a concrete case of God bearing witness together with the preachers.
Paul tells Timothy not to neglect his gift, using the same verb as Hebrews 2:3. It shows that neglect, an ordinary failure of care, is a recognised danger for believers, even those who are gifted.

The following warning names the end of the road that drifting leads to, a heart of unbelief that turns from the living God. It also gives the remedy: exhort one another daily, so that none is hardened by sin's deceitfulness.
The person who sinned defiantly despised the word of the LORD and was cut off. It stands behind the old penalties the writer has in mind, and shows what 'just punishment' under the law could mean.

The Spirit distributes gifts as He determines. It matches the phrase 'according to His will' in verse 4, and shows that the gifts that confirmed the gospel flowed from the Spirit's choice and not from human control.

What the salvation actually is: the Son shared our humanity so that by His death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death and free those enslaved by fear. It fills in the greatness of the salvation that verse 3 has only named.

study.oneStory:
The Bible is the story of God speaking and of people hearing or refusing to hear. In the garden, God's word was clear, and the first sin was a failure to trust it, Genesis 3:1-6. Ever since, the problem has been less that people lack words from God than that they do not take them in. Israel at Sinai heard God's voice and promised, 'All the words that the LORD has spoken, we will do,' Exodus 24:3, and within weeks they had made a golden calf. The prophets, century after century, were sent to people whose ears were closed.

Hebrews 2:1-4 stands at a particular point in that story. The speaking has now come to its fullest form in the Son, as chapter 1 declared, and the writer asks what a people should do with it. The answer is that they should attend, and not drift. The sin the passage fears is the quiet one that undoes many, the failure to keep listening.

This passage also connects the story's two halves. The word at Sinai was given with angels and penalties, and it was good, but it could not bring the people into the promised rest. The new word comes with a Saviour, and it can. The writer will show in chapters 3 and 4 that the wilderness generation failed to enter because they did not trust the word they heard, and that the promise of rest still stands for those who do. The warning here is a doorway to that longer argument.

It also tells us where we live. The confirmation of the gospel by signs and gifts is a mark of the beginning of the age to come, 'the powers of the coming age,' Hebrews 6:5. The church lives between the Lord's first announcement and His return, with the Spirit given as a pledge, Ephesians 1:13-14. The time is one in which it is easy to grow sleepy, and that is why the New Testament again and again calls believers to stay alert, Mark 13:37.

The story ends with a people who hear and keep hearing. In the new creation, God's people will see His face and His name will be on their foreheads, Revelation 22:4, and the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it. The salvation announced by the Lord and carried by the apostles will reach its completion. The warning of Hebrews 2:1-4 exists so that every reader will be there.

quiz.q: What is the specific danger this warning names?

options.text: Drifting away, slowly slipping past what we have heard.
options.note: The verb pictures a boat carried off course, an unnoticed drift.
The peril here is quiet neglect and drift, not dramatic blasphemy.

options.text: Forgetting a few minor details of doctrine.
options.note: It is more serious than lost details; it is drifting from the gospel itself.

options.text: Being physically far from a church building.
options.note: The drift is spiritual, away from the message, not a matter of geography.

quiz.q: How does the writer argue that neglecting the gospel is so serious?

options.text: From lesser to greater: if breaking the law brought just punishment, neglecting the greater salvation is worse.
options.note: Verses 2 to 3 reason from the binding law to the greater salvation.

options.text: By saying the law never mattered at all.
options.note: The law was binding and just; the point is that the gospel is greater still.

options.text: By promising there are no consequences either way.
options.note: The warning is precisely about inescapable consequences.

options.text: By claiming the gospel is easier to ignore safely.
options.note: The opposite: it is far more dangerous to ignore, being so great a salvation.

quiz.q: How was this great salvation confirmed?

options.text: Announced by the Lord, confirmed by those who heard Him, and attested by God with signs and gifts of the Spirit.
options.note: Verses 3 to 4 list the layers of confirmation.
It was confirmed by eyewitnesses and by God Himself.
It rested first on the Lord and eyewitnesses, attested by God.

options.text: By the angels who gave the law.
options.note: The angels gave the law; this salvation was announced by the Lord Himself.

quiz.q: What is the right response to this warning?

options.text: Pay closer attention to the gospel and hold fast, so as not to drift.
Assume grace covers all neglect, so relax.
options.note: Presuming on grace while drifting is the very danger warned against.

options.text: Add extra rules to feel more secure.
options.note: The call is to attend to the gospel, not to build new laws.

options.text: Wait passively to see what happens.
options.note: The call is active attention, not passive waiting.

questions: Drifting happens slowly and quietly. Where might you be slipping away from Christ without noticing?
The writer says to pay closer attention to what we have heard. What practical habits keep the gospel in front of you week by week?
This is called so great a salvation. Have you let it grow small and familiar, or does its greatness still move you?
God confirmed the gospel with eyewitnesses and signs. How does the solid, attested nature of the good news steady your faith?
Who around you seems to be drifting, and how could you help them pay closer attention rather than slip away?

translationNotes.note: The verb rendered 'drift away' is a nautical and everyday image for slipping past or being carried off course; it stresses gradual, unintended loss rather than a sudden decision.
'The message spoken by angels' refers to the giving of the law at Sinai, which Jewish tradition associated with angelic mediation; 'binding' translates a term for what is legally firm and valid.
'Confirmed to us by those who heard Him' indicates the writer and readers received the gospel from eyewitnesses of the Lord, placing them in a second generation of believers.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Hebrews 2:1-4. This is the first of the five warning passages; the strongest orthodox views are represented fairly. Sermon set to none; no expositor series confirmed this session.
